## Beats

### B00 · INTRO — cold open
**Pattern:** `ClaudeComposerAsk` (reuse) · **Motion:** type-on

> Hi, I am Simba. Every time a language model answers you, it's actually doing two completely different jobs. First it reads your entire prompt, all at once. Then it writes the reply, one word at a time. Those two jobs load the GPU in opposite ways — and mixing them badly is one of the biggest reasons a server ends up slow.

**On screen:** ask types in — "Why does a model feel instant on a long prompt, then trickle out its answer word by word?"; output lines land answered:
- "reading your prompt: one parallel pass, compute-bound"
- "writing the reply: one token at a time, memory-bound"

![B00 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B01 · SUMMARY — BLUF
**Pattern:** `ClaudeStatement` (reuse) · **Motion:** fade

> Prefill reads your whole prompt in a single parallel pass across every input token. Decode writes the reply one token at a time, each one waiting on the last. Same model, same GPU — two completely different kinds of work.

**On screen — kicker:** THE SPLIT · **sparkLine:** One phase is bottlenecked by compute. The other is bottlenecked by memory. They rarely bottleneck at the same time.

![B01 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B02 · STRUCTURE — what prefill actually does
**Pattern:** `ParallelPass` (new) · **Motion:** illustrate

> Prefill looks at every token in your prompt at the same time — a hundred tokens or a thousand, it's one forward pass either way, computed as one big matrix multiplication. Every input token feeds into that single pass at once, and it fans back out into two things: a KV cache entry for every token, and the first token of the reply.

**On screen:** a genuine fan-in/fan-out diagram — the prompt's tokens sit in a row at top, each with a line converging down into one wide terracotta-bordered box ("ONE FORWARD PASS — ALL TOKENS AT ONCE"), which then fans back out via two lines into two boxes below: "KV CACHE BUILT" (one entry per input token) and "FIRST TOKEN OUT" (the reply begins).
- **kicker:** PREFILL — ONE PARALLEL PASS OVER THE WHOLE PROMPT
- **tokens:** the prompt's tokens, e.g. ["The", "quarterly", "report", "shows", "revenue", "up"]
- **passLabel:** one forward pass — all tokens at once
- **outputs:** [{label: "KV cache built", detail: "one entry per input token"}, {label: "first token out", detail: "the reply begins"}]
- **sparkLine:** A hundred tokens or a thousand — still one pass, one big matrix multiply.

![B02 preview](data:image/png;base64,)
### B03 · REASONING — why the bottleneck flips
**Pattern:** `FactStack` (reuse) · **Motion:** illustrate

> That shape is what decides the bottleneck. Prefill multiplies a big batch of tokens against the same weights at once — lots of math per byte of memory it touches, so the GPU's compute cores stay busy. Decode does the opposite: one token's worth of math, but it still has to pull in every model weight and the entire key-value cache from memory to do it. Almost nothing to compute, a lot to read. That's why prefill is called compute-bound, and decode is called memory-bound.

**On screen — kicker:** WHY THE BOTTLENECK FLIPS — ARITHMETIC INTENSITY · **facts:**
- prefill: many tokens share one pass through the weights — high math-per-byte, compute stays busy
- decode: one token's worth of math, but every weight and the whole KV cache still has to be read
- same hardware, opposite constraint — compute-bound vs. memory-bound

**closingLine:** Prefill is limited by how fast the GPU can multiply. Decode is limited by how fast it can read.

![B03 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B04 · STRUCTURE — decode's loop
**Pattern:** `AutoregressiveLoop` (new) · **Motion:** illustrate

> Decode's loop never changes shape: take the last token and the cache built so far, run one forward pass, get the next token out, append it to the cache, and do it again. Every step depends on the step before it — there's no way to skip ahead or run two steps at once for the same reply. And the cache it reads from grows by exactly one block, every single time around.

**On screen:** an actual loop diagram — three boxes left to right ("last token + KV cache in" → "one forward pass" → "next token out"), connected by straight arrows, with a curved terracotta arrow arcing from the last box back underneath the row to the first, labeled "append to cache → repeat." Below the arc, a row of small blocks fills in left to right, one per cycle, the newest one always terracotta — the KV cache growing a block per step.
- **kicker:** DECODE'S LOOP — ONE STEP AT A TIME
- **stepIn / stepPass / stepOut:** last token + KV cache in / one forward pass / next token out
- **repeatLabel:** append to cache → repeat
- **cacheLabel:** KV CACHE
- **cacheBlocks:** 6 (illustrative — grows by one per real decode step)
- **sparkLine:** Every step depends on the step before it — there's no skipping ahead.

![B04 preview](data:image/png;base64,)
### B05 · RESULTS — what gets measured
**Pattern:** `DataTable` (reuse) · **Motion:** illustrate

> Servers measure these two phases separately. Time to first token is how long prefill takes — it grows with how long your prompt is. Time per output token is how long each decode step takes — it barely changes with prompt length, but it's set by how much has to be read from memory every single step.

**On screen — title:** WHAT GETS MEASURED · rows: TTFT — time to first token → prefill latency; scales with prompt length · TPOT — time per output token → decode latency per step; set by memory bandwidth, not prompt length · **footnote:** Sarathi-Serve, OSDI 2024 · DistServe, OSDI 2024 · **sparkLine:** Two different clocks, two different levers to pull.

![B05 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B06 · REASONING — what goes wrong sharing one GPU
**Pattern:** `FactStack` (reuse) · **Motion:** illustrate

> Put both phases on the same GPU without care, and they fight. A big prefill batch can hog the GPU for the time it takes to finish, and every decode step waiting behind it in the queue stalls until it's done — a new prompt showing up mid-conversation can freeze everyone else's reply. That's not a bug in one phase — it's the two bottlenecks colliding.

**On screen — kicker:** WHAT GOES WRONG SHARING ONE GPU · **facts:**
- a big prefill batch can hold the GPU until it finishes
- every decode step queued behind it stalls until the prefill clears
- one new prompt mid-conversation can freeze everyone else's reply

**closingLine:** Not a bug in either phase — the two bottlenecks colliding on one piece of hardware.

![B06 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B07 · FINDINGS — fix one, chunk the prefill
**Pattern:** `FindingPair` (reuse) · **Motion:** illustrate

> One fix keeps them on the same GPU, but schedules around the collision. Sarathi-Serve splits a big prefill into small chunks, and slots each chunk between ongoing decode steps instead of running it all at once. No decode ever waits for a whole prefill to clear — and that alone bought two-point-six to five-point-six times the serving capacity of vLLM, depending on the model.

**On screen:**
- **kicker:** FIX ONE — CHUNK THE PREFILL
- Finding 1 — "STALL-FREE SCHEDULING" / "A big prompt is split into small chunks, each one slotted between ongoing decode steps instead of running all at once." / stat: **Sarathi-Serve**
- Finding 2 — "SERVING CAPACITY" / "2.6× on a single GPU (Mistral-7B), up to 5.6× with pipeline parallelism (Falcon-180B), measured against vLLM." / stat: **2.6–5.6×**

![B07 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B08 · FINDINGS — fix two, don't share the GPU
**Pattern:** `FindingPair` (reuse) · **Motion:** illustrate

> The other fix doesn't share the GPU at all. DistServe runs prefill and decode on separate pools of GPUs entirely, each one tuned to its own bottleneck instead of splitting one GPU's time between two different jobs. Against the same latency bar, that served seven-point-four times more requests, while hitting a twelve-point-six times tighter deadline on over ninety percent of them.

**On screen:**
- **kicker:** FIX TWO — DON'T SHARE THE GPU AT ALL
- Finding 1 — "DISAGGREGATED SERVING" / "Prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, each tuned to its own bottleneck instead of splitting one GPU's cycles." / stat: **DistServe**
- Finding 2 — "MORE REQUESTS, TIGHTER DEADLINES" / "7.4× more requests served, hitting a 12.6× tighter SLO on over 90% of them, against the same latency bar." / stat: **7.4×**

![B08 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

### B09 · SUMMARY — verdict
**Pattern:** `ClaudeVerdictArtifact` (reuse) · **Motion:** stagger

> So: every reply is two jobs, not one. Prefill reads your prompt in one compute-bound pass; decode writes the reply memory-bound, one token at a time. Left alone on shared hardware, they collide — and two different fixes, chunking the prefill or splitting the GPUs entirely, both turn that collision into serving capacity, because they stopped treating one bottleneck like the other.

**Artifact lines:**
- Delivered: two-phase model — prefill reads the prompt in one compute-bound pass, decode writes the reply memory-bound, one token at a time.
- Proven: chunked prefill (2.6–5.6× capacity) and disaggregated serving (7.4× more requests, 12.6× tighter SLO) both convert the mismatch into gains — independently, in two separate systems.
- NOT fixed: decode's per-step ceiling — still one token at a time, still bound by how fast the GPU can read the KV cache.

![B09 preview](data:image/png;base64,)

## Sources
- Agrawal et al., "Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve," OSDI 2024 ([arXiv:2403.02310](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310); builds on Agrawal et al., "SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills," [arXiv:2308.16369](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16369)) — the compute-saturated/high-latency description of prefill vs. the low-utilization/low-latency description of decode (B02–B03), the chunked-prefill + stall-free scheduling mechanism (B07), and the 2.6×/3.7×/5.6× serving-capacity figures for Mistral-7B, Yi-34B, and Falcon-180B against vLLM (B07).
- Zhong et al., "DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving," OSDI 2024 ([arXiv:2401.09670](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670)) — the TTFT/TPOT framing (B05), the prefill-decode interference/colocation problem (B06), the disaggregated-serving mechanism (B08), and the 7.4× more-requests / 12.6× tighter-SLO / >90%-of-requests figures (B08–B09).
- The arithmetic-intensity framing (B03) — matrix-matrix vs. matrix-vector multiplication, compute-bound vs. memory-bandwidth-bound — is standard LLM-serving vocabulary used across both papers above and the wider vLLM/TensorRT-LLM serving literature; no single-paper figure is attached to it here, so no specific utilization percentage is claimed on screen.
- Continuity: `how-kv-cache-works` and `hai-paged-attention`, earlier videos in this series, are referenced directly in B04's sparkLine — decode's per-step read of the KV cache is exactly what PagedAttention's block table manages.
